title: Lehna becomes Angad
hook: Nanak names Lehna his successor and calls him Angad, part of my own body

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sheet of flowers, phull, and a Guru who belonged to no one side. Flowers for everyone.

Guru Nanak had two grown sons. The elder, Sri Chand, was deeply devout, an ascetic who had renounced ordinary life. The younger, Lakhmi Das, was a householder with a family. When a founder steps down, the next in line can seem obvious, the way the eldest son takes over the family shop. Either son would have been the obvious choice. But for years Nanak had been watching someone else: the trader who carried the wet grass, cleared the ditch and fished the bowl out of dirty water. So step back a little in time, to a few months before the flowers, and the day Nanak made his choice.
screen: `EVERYONE ASSUMES THE SON.` → `TWO SONS, BOTH DEVOUT.` → `THE GURU WAS WATCHING SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Nanak placed a coconut and five copper coins before Lehna and bowed to him. The teacher bowed to the student. Then he gave him a new name: Angad. Today's word is inside it. Ang means a limb, a part of the body, so Angad is often explained as part of my own body. This man isn't my replacement, the Guru was saying; he's me, continued. A ballad in the scripture, sung by two of the Gurus' musicians, Satta and Balvand, says it plainly: the light was the same, the way was the same; the king had only changed his body. That's the Sikh understanding of the ten Gurus. Not ten teachers with ten different messages, but one light passed from one body to the next, like a flame lit from a flame. That's why the Gurus whose hymns are in the scripture signed them not with their own names but with Nanak's. The word takes one more turn. Ang also names the pages of the Sikh scripture. You don't say page 360 of the Guru Granth Sahib; you say Ang 360. Each page is a limb of the Guru. The word that named the second Guru now names every page of the book Sikhs call their Guru today. And notice: Nanak didn't choose by blood. He chose the one who had become a servant. The light went to the one who could carry it, and it's still traveling.
screen: `THE TEACHER BOWED TO THE STUDENT.` · `ANG — A LIMB, PART OF THE BODY.` · `ONE LIGHT, A NEW BODY.` · `ANG — EVERY PAGE OF THE SCRIPTURE.` · then, large: `PASSING THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Think of something you care about: a skill, a family recipe, a way of doing your job, a value your parents gave you. Then see the face of whoever might carry it after you, a child, a colleague, a friend, a student. If nobody comes to mind, notice that too, and wonder who it might be.
Ang. A limb, a part of the body; inside the name Angad, and the word Sikhs use for every page of their scripture. Today's word.
Your line: passing the light. Tomorrow, the letters Guru Angad taught at Khadur. Day forty-four, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs understand the ten Gurus as one light passing through ten bodies, and they refer to the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib as angs, limbs of the Guru; Guru Angad's accession is remembered each year.

notes: Coconut and five copper coins (paise) placed before Lehna: common tradition; Bhai Buddha applying the tilak is omitted. Confirm.
Satta and Balvand's var line 'joti oha jugati saai sahi kaaiaa pheri paltteeai' at Ang 966; paraphrased. Confirm Ang.
Etymology: Angad commonly explained as 'part of my own body' (ang + ad/apna); confirm the explanation.
Date of succession (1539, shortly before Nanak's death) left unstated; 'a few months before the flowers' is approximate. Confirm.
Sri Chand described as ascetic (founder of the Udasi order, not named here); Lakhmi Das as householder. Confirm.
